Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs
The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation

Steve Brown ††thanks: orcid 0009-0009-1720-1785. With implementation and drafting assistance from Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI). Artifact availability: the merge operator, the divergence benchmark (benchmark/mergebench/) and the recorded-divergence replay corpus (benchmark/replay/) behind every number reported here are in the development repository, github.com/intigraph/quipu. Each result table names the command that regenerates it.
11 November 2026
Abstract

Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides’ changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result.

We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store’s Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies.

Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 3333 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 3333 conflicts but asked 845845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105105 human alias repairs (9393 after excluding 1212 chained pairs) and 939939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (00 of 9393 alias repairs detected, matching 00 of 2121 synthetic cases).

In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 2323 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.

1 Introduction

A knowledge graph that more than one writer can edit will diverge, and something has to put it back together. The obvious move is to reuse the tooling that already solves this for source code: keep the graph in a file, keep the file in git, and let a line merge reconcile two versions.

That move fails in a specific and instructive way. A line merge understands a document as an ordered sequence of lines, and a graph is neither ordered nor a sequence. Two writers who add unrelated facts about the same entity produce adjacent edits and a textual conflict. Two writers who re-serialize the same unchanged graph produce a diff of everything. Meanwhile a writer who sets a second value on a property the ontology says holds exactly one — the change that genuinely cannot be reconciled without a decision — produces a clean, conflict-free merge, because the two values live on different lines and nothing in the file says they compete.

The failure is not that line merge is bad at graphs. It is that conflict is a semantic property of the data model, and a line merge is being asked to infer it from a syntactic one. Our position is that an RDF merge should take conflict from the place the data model already defines it: the schema.

This paper.

We describe an operator with two halves. Triples are canonicalized and merged as sets, so serialization order cannot manufacture a conflict. A SHACL shapes graph then decides which slots the set algebra is allowed to settle on its own: where a shape bounds a slot’s cardinality and the two sides’ changes cannot both stand within that bound, the operator refuses and records a decision; everywhere else, it unions. Because the shapes are already present — they are what validates writes into the store — the merge policy is not a second configuration to keep in step with the ontology. It is the ontology.

What we are not claiming.

Three-way merge over canonicalized RDF is not new, and we searched before writing. Quit Store [1] places RDF under git with merge strategies, including a Context Merge that identifies conflicts by node overlap and refers them to a person; TerminusDB offers diff and patch over a versioned graph; RDF Patch and LD Patch standardize change description; RDFC-1.0 gives canonical labeling for graphs with blank nodes, which we build on rather than beside. To our knowledge — and scoped to that search — what has not been reported is an evaluation of SHACL-derived conflict semantics against those neighbors in a deployed system. That evaluation is the contribution, and the framing of the operator as an extension of Context Merge rather than a replacement for it is deliberate.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    A three-way merge operator over canonical triples whose conflict predicate is derived from SHACL cardinality, with post-merge validation against the same shapes, implemented in a production store (§3, §4).

  2. 2.

    A divergence benchmark with an oracle recomputable by a reader from published data alone, scoring eight strategies under one accounting contract, and a result that contradicts one of our own hypotheses (§5).

  3. 3.

    A replay of recorded multi-agent divergence from a production graph against the shipped operator, which reproduces the synthetic arm’s blind spot on real data and quantifies the benefit on a class that production surfaced nothing of (§6).

  4. 4.

    A study of evolving shape contracts that merges the declarations before the data, which handles the tested cardinality changes and shows that a datatype change escapes the conflict detector and is caught only by post-merge validation (§7).

  5. 5.

    Two checks that do not read the shapes: a use-case oracle run against the shipped operator, and a re-judging of the benchmark under deliberately wrong shapes, which shows that a missing bound loses data silently while a spurious one only costs questions (§8, §5).

  6. 6.

    A stated limit — alias divergence is invisible to triple-level merge — reported as a measured false-negative column rather than excluded from the benchmark, with a separate entity-resolution stage tested against it (§9).

2 Background

The unit of change.

An RDF graph is a set of triples. Two serializations of one graph may differ in every byte — Turtle groups by subject, N-Triples does not, and neither fixes an order within a group. A diff over serialized text therefore reports differences that do not exist in the data. Taking the triple as the unit of change removes that entire category: a three-way merge becomes set algebra over (Gb,Go,Gt)(G_{b},G_{o},G_{t}), and no result depends on how any side chose to write its file.

Blank nodes are the exception, since they have no stable name across serializations. RDFC-1.0 (formerly URDNA2015) assigns canonical labels and makes graph-level equality decidable. Our operator sits on top of that substrate; the benchmark in §5 uses ground graphs only, so it does not exercise blank-node canonicalization and is not evidence about it.

Where conflict comes from.

Set algebra alone answers only part of the question. If both sides add a triple, the union holds both. That is correct for a person’s email addresses and wrong for their date of birth, and nothing in the triples distinguishes the two cases. The distinction is in the schema: a SHACL shape [5] with sh:maxCount 1 on a property path states that the slot holds at most one value. A merge that unions into such a slot has not resolved the divergence; it has produced a graph that violates the very constraint the store enforces on ordinary writes.

This gives a conflict predicate with three properties we care about. It is declared, not inferred from edit patterns. It is already present, because the shapes are what the store validates against. And it is auditable, because the same shapes graph can be run over the merge output — so the definition of a conflict and the test for a bad resolution are one artifact rather than two that can drift apart.

Shares.

The operator reconciles share bundles: a directory holding a canonical N-Triples export, the shapes that govern it, and a manifest carrying a content hash of the graph and the identifier of the share it was derived from. The parent pointer is what supplies GbG_{b}, so fork-point anchoring is by content hash rather than by wall-clock time or by a centrally-issued sequence number. Two peers who have never spoken can therefore establish a common ancestor from the bundles alone.

3 The operator

Let GbG_{b}, GoG_{o} and GtG_{t} be sets of canonical triples, and let SS be a SHACL shapes graph. A slot is a pair (s,p)(s,p) of subject and predicate; we write G⁡[s,p]={o:(s,p,o)∈G}G[s,p]=\{\,o:(s,p,o)\in G\,\} for the values a graph carries in a slot. The slot is the unit of conflict because it is the unit sh:maxCount is declared over.

Additions and removals.

Each side’s change relative to the base is Ax=Gx∖GbA_{x}=G_{x}\setminus G_{b} and Rx=Gb∖GxR_{x}=G_{b}\setminus G_{x} for x∈{o,t}x\in\{o,t\}. These are exact: no heuristic decides whether a triple was “modified” rather than removed and re-added, because at triple granularity there is no such distinction to make.

Bounded slots.

Let 𝑚𝑎𝑥S​(s,p)\mathit{max}_{S}(s,p) be the maximum cardinality SS declares for pp on ss, or ∞\infty where none is declared. A slot is a candidate only when both sides changed it and disagree:

Go​[s,p]≠Gt​[s,p]∧Go​[s,p]≠Gb​[s,p]∧Gt​[s,p]≠Gb​[s,p].G_{o}[s,p]\neq G_{t}[s,p]\;\wedge\;G_{o}[s,p]\neq G_{b}[s,p]\;\wedge\;G_{t}[s,p]\neq G_{b}[s,p].

For a candidate, let M⁡[s,p]M[s,p] be the slot’s three-way set merge: the base values neither side removed, together with the values either side added. The slot is contended when

|M⁡[s,p]|>𝑚𝑎𝑥S​(s,p)|M[s,p]|>\mathit{max}_{S}(s,p)

or when 𝑚𝑎𝑥S​(s,p)=1\mathit{max}_{S}(s,p)=1, the base held a value, and one side emptied the slot while the other replaced its value. The predicate therefore yields three classes, which the evaluation reports separately. Functional divergence: a slot bounded at one receives two different values. Cardinality overflow: a slot bounded at n>1n>1 would exceed nn once both sides’ additions are united. Delete/modify: one side deleted a functional value that the other replaced; the set merge is within the bound, so the count alone would let the replacement silently override the deletion. An unbounded slot is never contended.

Both sides must have moved. If only one side changed a bounded slot, the other side’s value is still the base value, there is no disagreement, and the change applies — a merge that stopped to ask about it would be charging a person for a decision nobody needs to make.

The merge.

If any slot is contended, the operator returns conflicts and writes nothing; each contended slot is reported with its base, ours and theirs values, and the declared cardinality that made it a conflict. Otherwise the result is

Gm=(Go∪Gt)∖(Ro∪Rt),G_{m}\;=\;\bigl(G_{o}\cup G_{t}\bigr)\setminus\bigl(R_{o}\cup R_{t}\bigr),

a retraction on either side being honoured against the other side’s retained triples. The transaction records both parent share identifiers, so the merge is itself provenance: the lineage of a merged graph is inspectable in the same way a merge commit’s is.

Two properties worth stating.

The operator never lands a value for a slot it flagged — a conflicted merge writes nothing at all — so it cannot score well by both refusing a decision and quietly resolving it. And because GmG_{m} is defined by set operations over canonical triples, it is commutative in GoG_{o} and GtG_{t} and independent of serialization.

Post-merge validation.

GmG_{m} is validated against SS. This is not belt-and-braces: it is the falsifiable form of the design claim. If conflict semantics really are derivable from cardinality, then a merge that consulted the shapes should not be able to produce a graph that breaks a sh:maxCount bound. The claim is scoped to that constraint: datatype, class and minimum-count constraints are outside the predicate, and §7 reports a datatype violation that only this validation step catches. Any violation in GmG_{m} is corruption the operator admitted without charging anyone for it, and §5 reports that column for every strategy precisely so the claim can fail.

4 Implementation

The operator ships in Quipu, a governed bitemporal RDF store, as share_merge (approximately 480 lines of Rust). It exposes two entry points. status loads an incoming bundle, resolves the common ancestor through the manifest’s parent pointer, and reports what each side added and removed together with the contended slots — without writing anything, so a peer can be inspected before it is merged. merge performs the algebra of §3 and commits, recording both parent share identifiers on the transaction.

Three implementation choices are worth naming because they affect what the evaluation can claim.

The shapes come from the bundle, not the store.

Cardinality is read from the shapes carried inside the share being merged, not from the local store’s copy. A peer’s constraints therefore travel with its data, and merging does not silently reinterpret their graph under our schema.

Conflict is reported at slot granularity, with its evidence.

A DecisionRecord carries the subject, the predicate, the declared maxCount, and the base, ours and theirs value sets. The person resolving it is not told that a conflict exists and left to find it; they are told which constraint made it one and what the three candidate states were.

The evaluated operator is the shipped one.

The benchmark of §5 contains its own reference implementation of every arm, including ours, so that all eight are scored under one accounting contract. The replay of §6 deliberately does not: it drives share_merge::{status,merge} through real bundles built by the production share path. This matters because a benchmark’s copy of an operator can agree with a benchmark’s copy of an oracle for reasons that have nothing to do with the deployed system.

5 Arm A: a synthetic divergence benchmark

Design.

One seeded base graph over a synthetic vocabulary is copied twice and edited independently — separate random streams, so neither side’s edits can be a function of the other’s — under a six-operation model: assert, retract, re-describe, re-type, alias-mint, node-add. An overlap parameter controls how often an edit targets a contended quarter of the entity set, so collision probability is set directly rather than left to chance. Eight strategies then merge (Gb,Go,Gt)(G_{b},G_{o},G_{t}) and are scored against one oracle. There is no language model anywhere in the loop; the writers are deterministic, so a run is its own ground truth.

The oracle is recomputable by a reader, with one stated exception.

For the three triple-visible classes of §3 (functional divergence, cardinality overflow and delete/modify), ground_truth derives the oracle from the three graphs and the shapes and nothing else — no edit log, no generator intent — so a reader holding only the published inputs recomputes them exactly, and a generator bug cannot hide inside them. An instrument control asserts precisely that and reports the count it recovered. The alias-mint class is the exception, and necessarily so: two names for one entity is by construction invisible in the triples (§9), so no oracle could recover it from them. Those slots come from the generator’s mint log. They are 2121 of the 5454 conflicts summed over the five seeds, and every arm in Table 1 detects 00 of them, ours included — so the class bounds the recall column and touches nothing else: no arm’s precision or true-positive count depends on a number the reader cannot recompute.

The accounting contract.

Every arm answers two questions whose answers are in tension. Human decisions is the number of slots it refused to settle; a refused slot is held at its base value in the output, so no arm can flag a conflict and land a value for it. SHACL violations counts violations in what it landed automatically, against the same shapes that defined the conflicts — corruption it admitted without charging anyone. Either can be driven to zero by sacrificing the other, so neither is reportable alone. Triples lost and triples spurious are the third leg, and they catch the arm that admits no corruption and asks no questions because it discarded one side’s work. Both are measured against the oracle’s merge, in which a true conflict is held at its base value. For an arm that asks, a change it deferred on a slot that was not a true conflict is therefore counted as lost or spurious: the change is waiting for a person, not destroyed.

Results.

Table 1 aggregates five seeds (1,7,42,99,20261,7,42,99,2026) at 200200 entities, 200200 edits per side (400400 in total) and overlap 0.50.5 — the harness defaults, so the command below reproduces it unchanged. Regenerate with just bench merge --seed <N>; the outputs of those five runs are committed under benchmark/mergebench/results/, and Tables 2 and 3 are read from them. Instrument controls with just bench merge --selftest (77 properties, non-zero exit on any failure).

Three readings matter.

The comparison with the nearest neighbor is not about detection.

Summed over the five seeds the oracle contains 5454 conflicts, of which 2121 are alias-mint and 3333 are visible at triple level. shape-aware raised exactly those 3333, with zero false positives at every individual seed. context-merge raised the same 3333 — identical recall, seed by seed — and 812812 others, for 845845 questions in total. Two qualifications belong beside that figure. The context-merge arm is our reimplementation of the overlap rule, and it counts one question per changed slot on a subject both sides touched; Quit Store presents its overlap as a review set rather than a question count, and a reviewer who settles a whole subject at once would face fewer prompts than 845845. And the ratio depends on how much the two sides overlap: rerunning the same five seeds at overlap 0.10.1, 0.30.3, 0.70.7 and 0.90.9 gives 821821 questions against 3131, 797797 against 2525, 899899 against 6060 and 983983 against 8989, a ratio between 11×11\times and 32×32\times. In those twenty further runs shape-aware raised all 205205 triple-visible conflicts with no false positive, while context-merge missed 55 of them; the identical detection reported above holds at overlap 0.50.5 and is not a general property of the overlap rule (benchmark/mergebench/results/overlap-*/). The schema does not find conflicts the node-overlap heuristic misses. It distinguishes the ones that need a person from the 812812 that do not, which is a 25.6×25.6\times difference in the quantity the operator is actually spending: attention.

The zero columns are not all worth the same.

union, lww-theirs and triple-3way each report 00 human decisions, and none of them resolved anything. union admitted 5353–7272 SHACL violations. lww-theirs admitted almost none — and silently dropped 77–1616 triples and fabricated 44–1010, which is what last-writer-wins looks like when you count what it discarded rather than what it complained about. Only shape-aware holds all three at zero while still asking.

A hypothesis of ours did not survive.

We predicted that canonicalization alone would materially beat non-canonical line merge. Against the re-serialized arm it does: unparseable output lines go from 116116–169169 to 00. Against a stably serialized Turtle file it does not. git-canonical raises more conflicts (106106–144144) than git-turtle-stable (4141–5959), because sorting scatters each subject’s triples into one sorted run where two sides’ additions land adjacent and collide, whereas subject-grouped Turtle absorbed them into a block. The honest statement is narrower than the hypothesis: canonicalization buys syntactic integrity and independence from serialization order, and it does not by itself reduce conflict count. It is a trade, and we report it as one.

The circularity, stated rather than managed away.

shape-aware and the oracle both read the same shapes graph, and for the triple-visible classes their rules coincide by construction. shape-aware’s precision of 1.0001.000 on this arm is therefore a property of the design, not evidence about it. We do not repair this by making the oracle cleverer, which would only move the coincidence somewhere less visible. We handle it in two ways: by reporting per-class results (Table 3) so a reader can see which rows are definitional, and by confining this arm’s contribution to the cost of the alternatives. The replay arm (§6) replaces the generated corpus with recorded divergence and the harness with the shipped operator, but its positive results are scored against the same shapes. The evidence that does not pass through the shapes is a separate, smaller arm (§8).

The shipped planner differs from the reference arm on one slot.

shape-aware in this benchmark is a reference implementation. The harness can also call the library’s own slot planner (unified-core, built with --features shacl,merge-benchmark). On four seeds the two are identical on every metric. On seed 11 they differ on one slot, bounded at four values, where one side is unchanged and the other alone holds five. The reference arm flags a conflict, as the design rule requires. The planner classifies the change as one-sided and offers no decision, so in the benchmark, which calls the planner without the store’s write gate, it scores 66 true positives where the reference scores 77 and admits one violation. Through the shipped paths the five values are never written: a store with the shape loaded refuses the write that would create that side, and when we built such a bundle by tightening the bound after the write, share_merge refused the whole merge and wrote nothing. The defect is therefore a missing decision, an all-or-nothing refusal where the rule calls for a question, and not a silent violation. The figures in Tables 1 and 3 are the reference arm’s.

Wrong shapes: what the circularity hides.

A second judge derives the truth from the three graphs and a separate declaration of each predicate’s intended cardinality, and never reads the shapes. With the shapes as published, its truth equals the generator’s on every seed and every count in Table 1 reproduces. That agreement is by construction, because the shapes state the intent, and we do not count it as new evidence. The measurement is what happens when the operator is told shapes that are wrong while the truth stays fixed (Table 4). A missing bound costs recall and admits violations of the intended cardinality into the merged graph, while precision stays at 1.0001.000: the operator looks perfect on what it flags and is silent on what it was never told. A bound that is too tight or should not exist costs precision, as extra questions, and corrupts nothing. The shipped planner raises far fewer under such bounds than the reference arm, 1414 false positives against 278278. We do not credit it for that: it considers a slot only when both sides changed it, which is the same classification that misses the one-sided overflow above. context-merge reads no shapes and is unchanged in every row, at 812812 false positives. Shape quality therefore transfers directly into merge quality, and asymmetrically.

6 Arms B and C: recorded divergence, shipped operator

The synthetic arm can measure what the alternatives cost. It cannot be evidence that our operator is correct, because its oracle and its operator share a definition. This arm removes one half of that circularity and not the other. The incidents are recorded production divergence rather than generated: which names were later declared one entity, and which subjects carried doubled values and how many. The operator under test is the shipped share_merge driven through real bundles, so a disagreement between operator and expectation is a finding rather than a harness bug. The triples that carry each incident into a merge are constructed by the replay harness from those identities and multiplicities, with placeholder values; this arm replays recorded incidents, not recorded edit histories. The judgement, however, is still derived from the shapes. A comment-double decision counts as correct only because the description predicate carries sh:maxCount 1, and SHACL violations is scored against the same shapes in every arm. The one result in this arm that does not depend on the shapes is the alias column, and it is a negative: 00 of 9393. An oracle that does not read the shapes judges the same operator on a small set of cases in §8.

The corpus.

Extracted from a live multi-agent knowledge graph in which software agents and people had been writing concurrently for months, and committed as a fixture. Entity names are replaced by random labels and the mapping is discarded at build time; structure, cardinality and class membership are preserved exactly, and injectivity is verified over the 1,0761{,}076 names. Two divergence classes were recorded.

Alias-mint: two names silently minted for one entity, later repaired by a person asserting owl:sameAs. There are 171171 raw sameAs edges, which reduce to 105105 distinct undirected repairs (6666 edges were one repair recorded twice). Each is one repair a person actually performed — the manual-effort baseline. The class splits, and the split matters: 5252 of the 105105 are id-form, two spellings of the same commit identifier, which a normalization rule could retire without asking anyone; the other 5353 are two English phrasings of one concept, where nothing but a person can decide. Reporting 105105 as one undifferentiated “human decisions” figure would overstate the irreducible cost roughly twofold.

Comment-double: a sh:maxCount 1 description predicate that the production append path doubled instead of replacing — 939939 affected subjects carrying 1,7841{,}784 excess values.

Results.

Table 5 reports the replay. Regenerate with cargo run --example replay --features shacl.

The operator is blind to the entire alias class: 00 of 9393.

This reproduces the synthetic arm’s 00 of 2121 on alias pairs a person actually repaired, and it is the honest false-negative column. The zero follows from the structure of the case, since two different names share no slot, so it demonstrates a limit rather than measures a rate. Two names for one entity is invisible to any triple-level operator, shape-aware included; no schema fixes it, because it is a limit of the medium the operator works in.

The operator raises 939939 decisions on a class production surfaced none of.

The same class produced 1,7841{,}784 silent excess values through the append path. This is a counterfactual and must be read as one (§9).

A repair survives a concurrent edit.

owl:sameAs carries no cardinality constraint, so a repair asserted on one side unions rather than racing an edit to the aliased node on the other. A merge that could drop repairs would make the repair path itself unreliable, so this outcome is the wanted one rather than an incidental one.

The negative control.

Rerunning with the description predicate’s maxCount unbound takes comment-double from 939939 decisions to 00, everything merging cleanly. The decisions are therefore shape-derived — not manufactured by the harness — and this control arm doubles as the closest thing to a simulation of the production append path: it reproduces the doubling. That is the paper’s thesis stated as an experiment. Unbind the constraint and the conflict ceases to exist; the schema is what made it one.

Arm C: share, diverge, reconnect.

A case study walks the full lifecycle on a real bundle and verifies all eight hops: share a base bundle; a peer publishes a divergent share naming it as parent; we edit locally; status before reconnect reports diverged with +40+40 triples each side and 00 conflicts; the merge asserts 4040 and retracts 00; the transaction records two parents; both sides’ work is present afterwards (40/4040/40 each); and status after reconnect reports nothing outstanding. One detail is worth carrying: the graph hash is stable across runs while the share identifier is not, because the manifest embeds a timestamp. Fork-point anchoring depends on the graph hash, so lineage is unaffected — but a share identifier must not be used as a content identity.

6.1 Arm D: pairwise identity proposals

A preregistered follow-up tests whether Jev 1.13.0, TypeSafe AI’s hosted decision model that returns typed answers and probabilities rather than generated text [10], can propose identity decisions for the 9393 aliases missed by the triple-level operator. Given a pair, it returns same, different, or cannot_tell; the latter and confidence below .75.75 abstain. A proposal never applies an identity merge. The free comparators use normalized label edit similarity, MiniLM cosine, their union (all at .90.90), and a conservative explicit repository/commit-ID control. Thresholds and prompts were frozen before paid inference.

Evidence comes from preserved ROOT assertions before each pair’s earliest recorded transitive identity connection, with both transaction and valid-time restrictions. Identity annotations are stripped; current text and vectors do not fill missing historical evidence. Only 60/9360/93 positives have mechanically eligible evidence (39/4639/46 id-form, 21/4721/47 semantic). All original positives remain in recall; we also report recall among eligible positives.

Same-type neighbors ranked by maximum label/cosine score supplied proposed negatives, independently adjudicated using distinctness evidence. There are 114/46=2.478114/46=2.478 negatives per id-form positive and 41/47=0.87241/47=0.872 per semantic positive, short of the respective 3:13{:}1 targets by 2424 and 100100. Overall 155155 negatives exceed the 9393 floor but miss the 279279 target by 124124; one semantic negative exceeds the request-size cap. The reviewed semantic pilot negatives have clearly different descriptions, limiting hard-negative claims.

Pilot and availability.

The ten-item pilot produced eight typed responses and two client timeouts. After a first timeout at 30.15830.158 seconds, a registered amendment raised the client deadline from 3030 to 120120 seconds. Four responses took 0.3280.328–1.4181.418 seconds, followed by another timeout at 120.115120.115 seconds. The first latency uses attempt time to durable error-receipt time; subsequent measurements use a monotonic timer. Size alone does not explain these events: 4,3554{,}355 bytes timed out, 5,4275{,}427 bytes succeeded in 0.3440.344 seconds, and 5,5385{,}538 bytes timed out. A second public amendment allowed two retries for only the four untouched pilot negatives; all four responded on their first attempt. Earlier failures were retained, not retried. First-attempt and eventual item availability are both 8/108/10. The pilot recovered 2/32/3 id-form and 1/21/2 semantic positives, with one unavailable positive and one abstention; its four responding negatives produced no false identity proposals.

The held-out run used 204204 untouched eligible items, at most three attempts per item, 120120 seconds per attempt, a 612612-attempt cap and a $0.20 allowance. The first-5050 stop gate passed: first-attempt availability 48/5048/50, eventual availability 50/5050/50, requiring 5252 attempts. Valid abstentions count as available responses but not recovered aliases.

The completed held-out run used 216216 attempts; first-attempt availability was 192/204192/204 and eventual item availability 204/204204/204. Including the pilot, returned usage implies a list-price subtotal of $0.014897148; 14 attempts have unknown possible charges. Total account spend is therefore unknown. The local guard reserved $0.001 per unknown or in-flight attempt in addition to known usage; this is not a certified debit bound.

Held-out results.

Table 6 keeps pilot items separate and retains unavailable evidence in the original-positive denominator. False proposals are the errors that would collapse distinct entities if accepted; actual merges are zero in every arm.

Across pilot and held-out items, Jev recovered 14/9314/93 aliases; this is partial recovery of the operator’s 0/930/93 gap, not end-to-end entity resolution. On held-out positives it recovered 11/8811/88 overall, with one false identity proposal. The gains are predominantly id-form: the commit-ID control recovers ten held-out aliases without paid inference. On semantic positives Jev recovers one, versus three for label matching; the pilot is too small to reverse that conclusion. The preregistered requirement to beat the free baselines fails on the semantic stratum: this is a negative finding for Jev at the registered operating point, not evidence for adding a paid resolution step. Precision, abstention rates and threshold curves are released in the offline artifact; shared endpoints and selected negatives limit population inference.

Held-out Jev precision is 10/1010/10 for id-form and 1/21/2 for semantic proposals. Among eligible items, decision abstentions are 43/14743/147 id-form and 21/5721/57 semantic; another 77 and 2727 items respectively were withheld during evidence preparation. The ten ID-form recoveries overlap the commit-ID control on only five pairs: equal recall does not mean identical decisions.

The false proposal illustrates the distinction the prompt asks for: one record names CPU thermal excursions, while the other names missing fan telemetry on the same host. They describe different failure modes even though their host and thermal context overlap. Jev proposed identity at confidence .77.77; both free similarity scores were below .90.90. This observed error, together with lower semantic recall than label matching, argues for reviewed proposals rather than automatic identity collapse. Structured-predicate checks found zero identity predicates in all 248248 frozen request states, with an injected-edge positive control detected; this control does not certify arbitrary prose.

7 Divergent shape declarations (Arm E)

All earlier merge arms hold the shape contract fixed. Arm E instead tests a research orchestration: merge the shape declarations as RDF under a fixed SHACL-SHACL meta-shape, validate that contract, then merge data under it and validate again. The actual library share-merge APIs perform both merges using real common-base envelopes. The meta-shape declares path, bound and datatype functional on property-shape nodes. Shape graphs have stable named nodes; neither blank-node correspondence nor general SHACL meta-validation is tested.

Five explicit fixtures cover tightening maxCount from two to one, loosening a one-value bound, adding a functional property, changing datatype from string to integer and removing a shape. Each is repeated with five seed identities. Left edits under the old contract and right under its changed contract; both source branches are checked valid under their own contracts. An independent positive control changes the same bound differently in both shape branches and requires a meta-conflict. Positive and negative validation controls prove the meta-contract is exercised.

The cardinality cases behave as the merged contract specifies, including conflicts appearing on tightening and dissolving on loosening/removal. Datatype evolution exposes a boundary: the shipped detector reads cardinality bounds, so it misses the incompatible left-side string in the new integer contract. Post-merge validation detects the violation. That rejection is not counted as conflict recall, and the invalid candidate must not be admitted by a pipeline that treats validation as a gate. Merely merging shape triples does not derive a complete conflict policy for every SHACL constraint.

Table 7 uses explicit fixture oracles and holds a conflicted slot at base for automatic-output accounting, matching Arm A. The library itself blocks the entire merge; this normalization is not partial application. The Context column is the same changed-subject overlap rule on these literal-only fixtures, not an execution of Quit Store. Five identities do not constitute five sampled schema-evolution workloads. The orchestration is an experimental driver, not a deployed schema synchronization or negotiation feature. Regenerate with just bench schema and just bench schema-report; benchmark/shapes/ publishes all three input graphs, changed contracts, expected outputs and actual results.

8 Arm F: an oracle that does not read the shapes

Every positive result so far is scored against the shapes that also define the conflict. This arm removes that dependence for a small set of cases. Each case is a fixture that states, for one slot, the base, ours and theirs value sets, the slot’s intended cardinality, the decision a person takes, and the expected outcome: the current facts, the history records with their valid intervals, and the ordered transaction trace. The judge compares those expectations with what the store holds after the merge. It reads no shapes graph and imports no merge code; the expectations were written from the design document before the adapter existed. A driver builds each run from the case inputs alone and never reads the expected outcome.

There are 2424 cases: clean one-sided and two-sided changes, convergent changes, deletions, each decision on a contended slot (ours, theirs, base, a new value, a refused attempt to keep both, and a deferred decision), and three transaction-time and valid-time reads of a decided merge. We ran them against two shipped paths in private scratch stores: share_merge, the operator of §6, and the fork-promote path that shares its slot planner.

On every case either path can reach, the facts and the history agree with the oracle (Table 8). The four trace differences on the share path have one cause. When a merge has nothing to apply, the operator still records one empty receipt transaction, and the fixtures expect no transaction. The design document states both, in different places; we report the disagreement as measured and did not change the fixtures to match the code. The case neither path reaches needs an empty base, which the adapter cannot write. The second unreachable case on fork-promote is a real difference between the paths: when both sides converge on a value, fork-promote records no conflict, so a person cannot then choose a different value, and the share path can.

As a control, four captures were scored against a different case’s expectations, and all four failed, so agreement is not an artifact of a judge that accepts anything.

What this arm does and does not establish.

It is the first evidence in this paper that does not pass through the shapes: the shipped operator produces the facts and history that an independently stated expectation asks for. It is small. The cases are single-slot and synthetic, written by the project that wrote the operator. List-valued slots and repeated merges are specified as fixtures but have no adapter yet, and the conflict report is checked only on contended slots. No case has one side alone exceed a bound, so this arm does not exercise the planner difference of §5. It does not re-judge the 3333 decisions of §5.

9 Limitations

Scope: less human attention, not general merge correctness.

The claim this paper supports is narrow. For slot-level cardinality conflicts, the operator asks a person fewer questions than the alternatives we measured, and it loses nothing silently. It is evaluated in one deployment, over one ontology family, with SHACL cardinality bounds as the only constraint that defines a conflict. It does not cover alias divergence (00 of 9393 detected), datatype or other SHACL constraints, lists and blank-node structures, or ontologies that diverge beyond the Arm E fixtures. Every precision and true-positive figure in §5 and §6 is relative to the shapes that also define the conflicts, so none of them is evidence of shape-independent correctness. The only such evidence is Arm F (§8): 2424 single-slot synthetic cases, written by the same project, with list-valued slots and repeated merges not yet covered. It does not re-judge the benchmark or the replay.

Alias divergence is invisible, and that is a property of the medium.

When two writers mint different names for one entity, the graphs disagree about the world while agreeing about every triple. No triple-level operator can see it, so a recall of 1.0001.000 is not achievable by anything in Table 1. We left the class in the benchmark deliberately: it is a real divergence defect in the recorded corpus (105105 repairs), and excluding it would have produced a shape-aware arm scoring 1.0001.000 on both precision and recall as an artifact of what we chose to measure. Arm D tests a separate pairwise entity-resolution stage, using labels and historical neighborhoods to propose identity decisions. Its held-out run recovered 11/8811/88 aliases (11/5511/55 with eligible evidence) and proposed one false identity. Semantic recall was 1/451/45 (1/191/19 eligible), compared with label matching’s 3/453/45 (3/193/19 eligible) and zero false proposals. The preregistered baseline-beating condition fails on this stratum, a negative finding for Jev. Candidate generation is a separate requirement whose recall bounds end-to-end resolution, and we measured it with free signals only. Each pair’s left endpoint ranks every entity asserting one of its types before the repair, by the larger of normalized label similarity and MiniLM cosine over the same cleaned pre-repair evidence, with ties counted against the true partner. Recall at k=1,5,10,50k=1,5,10,50 is 3838, 5454, 5656 and 5757 of 9393 (id-form 23,32,34,3523,32,34,35 of 4646; semantic 15,22,22,2215,22,22,22 of 4747). The ceiling is the type block, not the ranking: 3030 partners cannot be ranked at all, 2626 of them because they never enter the anchor’s typed pool (1515 had no pre-repair facts and 1111 carried disjoint types), and 2525 of the 3030 are semantic. Among the 6363 rankable partners, 5656 fall in the top ten, and cosine alone puts more partners first (4343) than the combined score (3838). A resolver fed by this blocker would lose about a third of all aliases, and over half of the semantic class, before pairwise resolution begins. Historical evidence gaps, the semantic negative shortfall, easy reviewed negatives, and shared endpoints limit generalization. No actual identities were merged, so the study measures proposed errors rather than downstream damage or the economic cost of accepting them.

The 939939 is a counterfactual.

Those doublings arose from sequential re-posts through a single write path, not from a share, a divergence and a merge. The supported claim is narrow: had the same edits arrived as a divergence and been reconciled by this operator, each would have been surfaced as a decision instead of silently doubling. It is not a claim that the operator was running and prevented 1,7841{,}784 doublings.

Comment bodies in the merge replay corpus are synthetic.

Real values are prose about a deployment. In arm B, only the incident identities and the multiplicity are real — which is all the merge reasons about, but it does mean the corpus cannot support any claim about value content.

A conflict blocks the whole merge, not the conflicting slot.

The operator returns conflicts with nothing asserted. On a slice like the 939939-subject one, a single reconnect writes nothing until every contended slot is resolved. This is the conservative choice and it is a real usability cost; partial application with a held-back conflict set is future work.

Ground graphs only.

The benchmark’s graphs contain no blank nodes, so canonicalization there reduces to sorting. RDFC-1.0 is the substrate we build on and is not exercised by this arm; nothing here is evidence about blank-node canonicalization.

Timing is indicative.

Arm A uses one machine, one process and single runs. The line-merge arms include process spawn for git merge-file, of order 55 ms, which dominates their timing at every size measured; those columns are not comparable with the in-process arms and we do not report them as if they were.

Slot granularity is an assumption.

A conflict is reported over a (s​u​b​j​e​c​t,p​r​e​d​i​c​a​t​e)(subject,predicate) slot because that is the unit sh:maxCount is declared over. An operator working at another granularity would need a different scorer, and the comparison in Table 1 would not transfer unchanged.

Evolving shapes need more than cardinality.

Arm E uses a small, fixed meta-contract over named shape nodes and an experimental orchestration, not a production schema negotiation protocol. Its datatype case is a detector false negative detected by validation; passing the shape-graph merge does not make all data changes under the new contract safe.

One deployment.

The recorded corpus comes from a single production store. Its class distribution — alias-mint and functional-value doubling dominating — may not generalize, and we make no claim about divergence rates in other systems from it.

How often production writes would have needed a merge is only sampled.

The deployment writes through one path, so its history contains overwrites and no merges. We counted the overwrites that look like concurrent edits in a read-only copy of the store: a single-valued slot replaced by a different value within 300300 seconds by a different declared writer. The count is a sample, not a census. It covers 299,026299{,}026 of 1,443,4901{,}443{,}490 transactions (20.7%20.7\%): the first 99,04899{,}048 consecutively, then one 2,0002{,}000-transaction window from each of 100100 equal strata. It found 1010 such pairs in the prefix and 1,3441{,}344 in the sample, almost all on work-item status, version and modification-time slots. In 1,2501{,}250 of the sampled pairs both writes carry the same recorded principal behind different declared names, and 8989 have different principals. These are physical value replacements; the base each writer read is not recorded, so none is shown to be a lost update, and uncovered history is unknown rather than zero (scripts/merge-shadow-census.py).

Private evidence limits inference reproducibility.

Arm D publishes the item labels, frozen free-baseline scores, prompt, numeric responses, attempt ledger, and offline scorer. Its structural item views replace private strings with random tokens and withhold descriptions; selected evidence examples are scrubbed editorial paraphrases. These artifacts reproduce scoring, not the original model requests or embeddings. Reviewer inspection used the preserved private evidence. A reader cannot independently regenerate the model outputs from the public views, and a commercial model may change separately. Timeouts may be billed without usage responses, so list-price subtotals do not establish total account spend. First-attempt and eventual-item availability must be reported separately when retries are allowed.

10 Related work

Git-backed RDF versioning.

Quit Store [1] is the closest neighbor and the reason this paper makes no priority claim. It places RDF under git — the system’s own gloss on its name is “Quads in Git” — versions quads with commit-level provenance, and supplies merge strategies, including a Context Merge that identifies conflicts by node overlap and hands them to a person. The triple-set framing of three-way merge is present there; we are not introducing it.

Our delta is where the conflict predicate comes from. Context Merge derives contention from the shape of the change: it marks the subject and object of every added or removed statement with the commit it came from, and a node marked by both sides becomes a conflict. We derive it from the shape of the data, as declared in SHACL. The difference is a deliberate design choice on their part rather than an oversight, and they state it: Quit Store declines to encode semantic rules and relies on the pure RDF data model instead, and it presents Context Merge as a supervised approach to identifying conflicts rather than as a decision procedure. Our claim is correspondingly narrow. SHACL is exactly the source of semantic rules they chose not to hard-code, and what lets us consult it is circumstance rather than insight: in a shapes-governed store those rules are already present, already authored by the people who authored the data, and already the contract the graph is validated against.

They go one step further than declining, and it is worth stating plainly because it is the closest any prior work comes to the idea in this paper: Quit Store’s discussion names SHACL itself, proposing that users define application-domain rules as ontological restrictions and that adherence to them be enforced by continuous integration over the repository. The placement is then the whole of our delta. There, shapes are a quality gate applied to a merge that has already happened; here, shape cardinality is the conflict predicate that decides what the merge is permitted to settle at all, and the post-merge check they propose is additionally what we run to audit the result (§3). This operator therefore does not introduce SHACL to RDF merging. It moves it from after the merge to inside it, and the 845845-against-3333 result below is the measurement of what that move buys.

The consequence is measurable rather than rhetorical, and it is the central result of §5: across five seeds the two approaches detect an identical set of 3333 triple-visible conflicts, and the context heuristic asks 845845 questions where cardinality asks 3333. Overlap is a good proxy for “these edits are related”, which is what Context Merge sets out to find. It is a poor proxy for “these edits cannot both be true”, which is the smaller question that actually needs a person — and Context Merge does not claim to answer it. The 845845 against 3333 therefore measures two different questions being asked, not one strategy failing at the other’s task: it quantifies what the extra information buys, and that information is only available to a merge that has a shapes graph to consult. We position this operator as an extension of that line of work: the algebra is theirs, the conflict predicate is the contribution.

Diff and patch over versioned graphs.

TerminusDB [9] provides diff and patch over a versioned graph store. RDF Patch and LD Patch standardize the description of change sets. These solve the representation and transport of a delta; they are complementary to, and do not decide, what makes two deltas irreconcilable.

Canonicalization.

W3C RDF Dataset Canonicalization [6] (RDFC-1.0, formerly URDNA2015) gives deterministic labeling of blank nodes and hence decidable graph equality. We build directly on it: it is what makes “the same triple” well defined across two independently serialized bundles, and it is a substrate rather than a competitor. R43ples [3] and archiving systems such as OSTRICH [8] address efficient storage and querying of revision histories, a different problem from reconciling two live divergent copies.

Convergent replicated types.

CRDT constructions for RDF, such as SU-Set [4], guarantee convergence without coordination. They and this operator make opposite trades deliberately. A CRDT resolves every case automatically, which requires that some rule always picks a winner; for a functional predicate whose two values are both asserted in good faith, any such rule silently discards somebody’s knowledge. We would rather stop and ask, and accept that this means a merge can fail. Where automatic convergence is required, a CRDT is the right tool and this is not; where the graph is a shared record of what is believed to be true, a silently dropped assertion is the more expensive failure. Operational transformation has the same shape of trade in a different lineage.

Schema-aware merging elsewhere.

Ontology alignment and matching address a related question — reconciling different conceptualizations — but operate on schema-to-schema correspondence rather than on three-way reconciliation of instance data under a shared schema. Structured merge tools for source code (semi-structured and AST merges) share our motivation exactly: raise the merge above lines to the level at which the medium defines conflict. Our claim is the RDF instance of that principle, with SHACL supplying the structure.

Evidence maintenance and reviewed agent memory.

Choudhary’s PolyGraph [2] records alternative evidence bundles for derived artifacts and audits receipts by re-derivation after evidence removal. Its abstract reports that deleting only directly extracted facts leaves substantial contamination. This is complementary to shape-aware merge: structural consistency does not establish that an artifact’s evidence remains sufficient after source withdrawal. We do not benchmark receipt fidelity here. Raj’s Plant Memory [7] combines rule-first extraction, optional LLM review, reified facts with evidence, confidence and verification state, technician review, and MCP access. Its abstract reports a synthetic 400-work-order evaluation. It is an application-specific reviewed memory system; our operator reconciles divergent RDF graphs under shared SHACL constraints. Neither abstract establishes a comparison of temporal or withdrawal semantics with this implementation, and we make no such claim.

11 Conclusion

Merging knowledge graphs by merging their text asks a line-oriented tool to infer a semantic property, and it fails in both directions: it manufactures conflicts from serialization order and misses the divergences that genuinely cannot be reconciled automatically. Taking the canonical triple as the unit of change removes the first failure entirely. Taking the conflict predicate from a SHACL shapes graph addresses the second, and does so without adding a policy that has to be maintained alongside the ontology — because it is the ontology, and the same shapes then audit the result.

The evaluation supports a narrow claim, which is the one we make. Against the nearest neighbor, schema-derived conflict semantics do not detect more: they detect the same 3333 triple-visible conflicts across five seeds while asking 3333 questions rather than 845845, with no triples lost, none fabricated and no constraint violations admitted against the same shapes. That is less human attention for cardinality conflicts, not general merge correctness; an oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of every reachable case among 2424 single-slot ones. Replaying scenarios built from 939939 recorded duplicate-value incidents and 9393 of 105105 recorded repairs (1212 chained pairs excluded) against the shipped operator reproduces that benefit on incidents nobody generated for the purpose — and reproduces the blind spot too: alias divergence is invisible to triple-level merge, 00 of 9393, and no schema will fix it.

The schema-evolution trials refine that claim. Merging declarations first changes cardinality decisions as intended in the tested fixtures, but datatype incompatibility still needs validation and a resolution policy. Schema-first orchestration is therefore not a complete conflict-resolution rule on its own.

Three directions follow. The use-case oracle covers single slots; extending it to lists, repeated merges and the benchmark’s own decisions would judge the operator independently of the definition it implements at scale. Partial application would let a merge land its uncontended slots and hold back only the contended ones, removing the cost noted in §9. And the alias class, which the recorded corpus shows is real and which this operator cannot see, is where entity resolution would have to meet merge — with the open question being whether its errors are cheaper than the divergence it repairs.
